papers.summary: This paper evaluates the effects of the European Union’s (EU) regional trade agreements (RTAs) on trade patterns, with a particular focus on diversification. Using a structural gravity model with data for 170 industries, we exploit variation in RTA depth, measured by the number of legally enforceable provisions, to estimate the effects of deep trade agreements, allowing for heterogeneity across sectors.

papers.title: Monetary policy surprises with imperfect information
papers.abstract: High-frequency interest rate surprises around Fed announcements do not identify monetary policy (MP) shocks if markets are imperfectly informed. Instead, they can also reflect central bank information (CBI) shocks, when the Fed assesses the economy differently, and Fed-response-to-news (FRN) shocks, when markets misperceive the policy rule. The literature treats these as competing explanations; we show they are distinct, and jointly identify all three from the co-movement of interest rate and equity surprises, their predictability from public news, and heteroskedasticity between FOMC and non-FOMC communication. CBI effects are robust at daily and monthly frequencies; FRN matters only daily. Purging both strengthens monetary policy estimates.
papers.summary: High-frequency interest rate surprises around Fed announcements do not identify monetary policy (MP) shocks if markets are imperfectly informed. Instead, they can also reflect central bank information (CBI) shocks, when the Fed assesses the economy differently, and Fed-response-to-news (FRN) shocks, when markets misperceive the policy rule.

papers.title: Forecasting wages with local linear forests
papers.abstract: This study applies a Local Linear Forest (LLF) for wage forecasting in France. The LLF outperforms benchmarks such as Random Walk (RW), Ridge Regressions (RR) and Random Forests (RF). We also show that adding foreign predictors (i.e. measures of real activity, price and wage pressures from Germany and Italy) to French economic variables significantly improves wage predictions in France. The implications of our results are that wage dynamics in France exhibit non-linearity, to a certain extent, and that the better ability of LLFs relative to RFs to fit smooth signals is a valuable feature, especially at times in which wage growth reaches unprecedented levels from an historical perspective.
papers.summary: This study applies a Local Linear Forest (LLF) for wage forecasting in France. The LLF outperforms benchmarks such as Random Walk (RW), Ridge Regressions (RR) and Random Forests (RF). We also show that adding foreign predictors (i.e. measures of real activity, price and wage pressures from Germany and Italy) to French economic variables significantly improves wage predictions in France.

papers.title: What Drives Policy Responses to the 2026 Energy Shock? First Evidence from the IMF Global Policy Tracker
papers.abstract: This paper examines the determinants of policy responses to the 2026 energy shock using the newly constructed IMF Global Policy Tracker. The main analysis focuses on measures announced between end-February and early June, while preliminary data through mid-September shed light on how policy responses evolved as energy prices began to normalize. The findings point to distinct drivers of policy composition and design. At average public debt levels, greater shock exposure is associated with a larger share of price pass-through measures. As debt rises, this association strengthens, while the relationship between exposure and fiscal shielding weakens. Monetary responses are driven mainly by pre-shock inflation developments, while financial-stabilization measures are more closely associated with reserve adequacy. Policy design—including targeting and temporariness—is shaped more by institutional capacity, inflation, and the political cycle than by shock exposure. The extended dataset shows a gradual shift away from fiscal shielding toward pass-through, demand- and inflation- management measures. Later announcements are more likely to identify beneficiaries but less likely to include explicit expiry dates or sunset provisions. The main findings broadly hold, although some become less statistically significant.
papers.keywords: Energy price shock; Middle East Conflict; Real-time policy tracker; Real-time surveillance; Policy response; Policy space
papers.summary: This paper examines the determinants of policy responses to the 2026 energy shock using the newly constructed IMF Global Policy Tracker. The main analysis focuses on measures announced between end-February and early June, while preliminary data through mid-September shed light on how policy responses evolved as energy prices began to normalize. The findings point to distinct drivers of policy composition and design.

papers.title: Inside Central Bankers’ Calendars: How Do Fed Chairs Allocate Their Time?
papers.abstract: How leaders allocate their limited time and attention is an important question in economics. This paper constructs and analyzes a novel data set covering the daily calendars of three Federal Reserve Chairs, Ben Bernanke, Janet Yellen, and Jerome Powell, containing more than 20,000 calendar entries. We document several patterns. First, all Fed Chairs spend more than 30% of their documented meetings with Fed staff, highlighting the crucial role of economists in the Fed's decision process. Second, interactions with the media became more frequent during Bernanke's tenure and remained important until the end of Powell's tenure. Third, Powell held significantly more meetings with lawmakers than both Yellen and Bernanke, reflecting an increasing need for the Fed to engage with political actors. Beyond these trend patterns, we examine the time allocation of Fed Chairs at business cycle frequencies and show how different activities respond to shifts in the macroeconomic environment. Finally, we place our findings in historical context using the available calendars of earlier Fed Chairs, including Alan Greenspan.

We document several patterns.

papers.title: Competitive Search for Bundles
papers.abstract: How does buyers’ search for bundles generate sorting among heterogeneous sellers? We study competitive search in which buyers assemble bundles through separate transactions, where prices direct search and determine congestion. With two seller types, buyers choose only same-type bundles below a single threshold in cross-type value and cross-type bundles above it. The threshold lies strictly between geometric and arithmetic means of same-type values, so search produces cross-type matching even when types are complements. With a continuum of types, log-supermodularity and submodularity yield unique stable equilibria with positive and negative assortative matching. Positive sorting extends to any fixed number of visits.

We study competitive search in which buyers assemble bundles through separate transactions, where prices direct search and determine congestion. With two seller types, buyers choose only same-type bundles below a single threshold in cross-type value and cross-type bundles above it.

papers.title: Fiscal-Monetary Interactions: The Role of Debt Maturity
papers.abstract: This paper examines how the maturity structure of sovereign debt shapes fiscal–monetary interactions in the United States. Using exogenous monetary policy shocks and nonlinear local projections, we show that debt maturity influences both the fiscal consequences of monetary tightening and its macroeconomic transmission. When the government relies more heavily on short-term debt, contractionary monetary policy shocks lead to large and persistent increases in public debt, more pronounced deteriorations in fiscal and financial conditions, and significantly larger declines in output, inflation, and private investment. These effects are substantially attenuated when debt maturity is longer. We rationalize the findings with a model in which a constrained intermediary holds both private credit and long-duration government debt and carries its bond portfolio at amortized cost. The intermediary’s opportunity cost of lending therefore depends in part on the yield locked in when the bonds were acquired, rather than solely on their one-period holding return, allowing sovereign debt maturity to directly influence the price of private credit.
papers.summary: This paper examines how the maturity structure of sovereign debt shapes fiscal–monetary interactions in the United States. Using exogenous monetary policy shocks and nonlinear local projections, we show that debt maturity influences both the fiscal consequences of monetary tightening and its macroeconomic transmission.

papers.title: Does Easy Money Win Elections?
papers.abstract: Governments press central banks for lower interest rates on the premise that easy money wins elections. We test this premise for 385 elections in 18 countries, 1900–2020, using exogenous interest rate changes. We find no evidence that monetary easing helps incumbents. At the point estimate, a typical easing leaves the incumbent’s vote share unchanged; the one-sided 95 percent confidence bound on the gain is 0.90 percentage points. Of 104 incumbent defeats, such an easing would have reversed none at the point estimate and 15 at the bound, all in close races. Easy money offers incumbents no reliable electoral return.
papers.keywords: Monetary policy; Central bank independence; political pressure; Economic voting; Political business cycles; Trilemma; JEL: D72; E52; E58; F42; N10
papers.summary: Governments press central banks for lower interest rates on the premise that easy money wins elections. We test this premise for 385 elections in 18 countries, 1900–2020, using exogenous interest rate changes. We find no evidence that monetary easing helps incumbents.

papers.title: Austerity and Productivity: Evidence from Euro Area Regions
papers.abstract: We find that fiscal consolidations raise productivity significantly and persistently. In our data, a consolidation that lowers regional public spending by 1% on impact raises TFP by about 1% on impact and about 2% after two years, even as economic activity contracts. We document this using two innovations. First, we build a novel regional utilization-adjusted TFP series for Europe, covering 139 NUTS 2 regions in ten euro area countries over 1999– 2019, which corrects the Solow residual for cyclical variation in capital utilization and labor effort. Second, we isolate plausibly exogenous spending cuts with a Bartik-style instrument that interacts pre-accession regional spending shares with narratively identified national consolidation episodes. Productivity gains are larger than those observed in comparable downturns without consolidation and arise almost entirely within sectors and coincide with net exit of establishments, rather than reflecting reallocation across sectors.
papers.keywords: Fiscal consolidation; Euro area; Total factor productivity; JEL: E32; E62; H53
papers.summary: We find that fiscal consolidations raise productivity significantly and persistently. In our data, a consolidation that lowers regional public spending by 1% on impact raises TFP by about 1% on impact and about 2% after two years, even as economic activity contracts. papers.title: Committee Deliberation and Gender Differences in Influence
papers.abstract: This paper provides empirical evidence on the aggregation of information in hiring committees. We use data from the hiring process of a large company in which committee members first conduct independent one-on-one interviews and then deliberate to reach a collective hiring decision. Results show that the mapping of committee members' initial assessments to final decisions is not deterministic, leaving scope for deliberation and individual influence. Committee decisions are systematically less aligned with recommendations made by women than with those made by men, despite similar qualifications, experience, and evaluation behavior. This gender difference in influence is strongest when disagreement is high and when women are in the minority. Further results suggest that it has implications for the gender composition of new hires.

We use data from the hiring process of a large company in which committee members first conduct independent one-on-one interviews and then deliberate to reach a collective hiring decision.

papers.title: The Depositary of Last Resort
papers.abstract: What are the consequences of making central bank deposits accessible to actors beyond the banking sector? We collect novel micro data on deposit accounts historically held with the Bank of England by individuals and firms other than banks to study their role in the financial panic of 1866. We document that the use of deposit accounts at the central bank soared during the crisis, while commercial banks permanently lost funding. The expansion in the number of active accounts was fueled by individuals, but the intensive margin increase in balances came almost entirely from firms. Recourse to central bank deposits was heterogeneous and persisted well beyond the panic, reflecting easy access, low opportunity costs, and positive network externalities. At the same time, retail borrowers seeking liquidity support from the Bank during the crisis preferred receiving loan proceeds in the form of cash rather than deposits.

papers.title: Artificial Intelligence and Climate Change: Balancing Innovation and Sustainability
papers.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is becoming an increasingly important factor in the climate transition. AI can improve energy efficiency, optimise resource use, accelerate climate innovation and strengthen climate forecasting, adaptation and risk management. At the same time, the development and deployment of AI require substantial computational resources, increasing electricity demand and, depending on the carbon intensity and timing of electricity use, associated emissions. We examine AI’s direct environmental footprint, its contribution to climate mitigation and adaptation, and rebound effects arising from lower costs, higher productivity and wider adoption. The overall impact of AI on climate change also depends on how AI capabilities evolve. We consider two stylised scenarios. Under an AI copilot scenario, benefits and environmental costs are likely to build up more gradually, but the net climate effect remains uncertain, depending on whether efficiency gains outpace growth in AI use, on the carbon intensity of additional electricity needed to power AI, and on how productivity gains translate into economic activity and resource use. Under a more transformative scenario involving artificial general intelligence (AGI), with cognitive capabilities comparable to those of humans across a broad range of tasks, both the potential benefits and environmental risks could become larger and more uncertain. The paper also reviews emerging policy responses and highlights the relevance of the AI–climate nexus for central banks. By affecting productivity, energy systems and climate-related risks, the AI–climate nexus can influence potential output and inflation dynamics, while the scale and financing of investment in AI and energy infrastructure may also have implications for financial stability.
papers.keywords: Artificial intelligence; Artificial General Intelligence; Climate change; Energy efficiency; Carbon emissions; geopolitical risk; JEL: O33; Q51; Q55
papers.summary: Artificial intelligence (AI) is becoming an increasingly important factor in the climate transition. AI can improve energy efficiency, optimise resource use, accelerate climate innovation and strengthen climate forecasting, adaptation and risk management.

papers.title: Transition Risk in Emerging Economies
papers.abstract: Many emerging economies tend to rely considerably on carbon-intensive sectors, exposing themselves to potential transition risk. This paper quantifies the impact of this risk and the role of various policies and policy designs in mitigating it. It does so with a two-country two-sector environmental dynamic stochastic general equilibrium model, where each “country” represents a bloc of advanced or emerging economies, respectively. The model includes real-world features such as financial frictions and financial and trade linkages across blocs. With it, we simulate climate policy in advanced economies, in the form of carbon taxes and tariffs, and international coordination around a minimum global carbon price. This paper identifies and quantifies important vulnerabilities among emerging economies to the implementation of climate policy in advanced economies.
papers.keywords: Transition risk; Emerging economies; Financial frictions; Environmental dynamic stochastic general equilibrium model; JEL: E44; E58; F38; F42; G18; O11; Q58
papers.summary: Many emerging economies tend to rely considerably on carbon-intensive sectors, exposing themselves to potential transition risk. This paper quantifies the impact of this risk and the role of various policies and policy designs in mitigating it.

papers.title: The Great Game: A Model of Geoeconomic Competition
papers.abstract: We build a model of two hegemons that have valuable trading relationships with each other and at the same time compete in exerting geoeconomic power over countries in the rest of the world. When the hegemons trade with each other, their optimal policy is shaped both by classic economic considerations - the profitability of that specific trade - and by geoeconomic competition - how the trade affects the power of each hegemon vis-a-vis the rest of the world. We show that containment, a policy mix in which a hegemon limits sales of its inputs to the rival hegemon and uses its power to demand that the rest of the world shift away from sourcing from the rival, arises when the two hegemons offer relatively substitutable exports, are less interdependent with each other, and have more direct geopolitical rivalry. Countries in the rest of the world benefit, all else equal, from hegemons containing each other since they partially squander their power with offsetting demands. However, containment policy can also worsen the efficiency of global production, leaving the rest of the world worse off.
papers.summary: We build a model of two hegemons that have valuable trading relationships with each other and at the same time compete in exerting geoeconomic power over countries in the rest of the world.

papers.title: Measuring Common Ownership: An Axiomatic Approach
papers.abstract: This paper proposes three basic axioms for measuring common ownership based purely on the ownership distributions: symmetry, normalization, and orthogonality. Combining a fourth, structural axiom with normalization yields a characterization of cosine similarity as the only commonality measure that satisfies all axioms. The paper also discusses how the basic axioms relate to measures of common ownership used in empirical research.
papers.keywords: Common ownership; Ownership concentration; Cosine-similarity; JEL: C43; D63; G34; L51
papers.summary: This paper proposes three basic axioms for measuring common ownership based purely on the ownership distributions: symmetry, normalization, and orthogonality. Combining a fourth, structural axiom with normalization yields a characterization of cosine similarity as the only commonality measure that satisfies all axioms.

papers.title: Political Ideology and Durable Spending
papers.abstract: Research in psychology suggests that conservatives should focus more on the investment value of durables, whereas liberals on consumption value. We test this hypothesis by examining the differential housing transaction motives of conservative and liberal households. Similar to other durable goods, housing assets embody both consumption and investment values and represent the largest assets of U.S. households. We show that conservative households transact more frequently than observationally similar liberal households, especially in secondary properties. Conditional on transacting, conservatives more often trade down and realize capital gains, while liberals trade up and increase housing consumption. Crucially, conservatives’ transactions are more sensitive to financial incentives affecting housing’s investment value: changes in interest rates, the opportunity cost of housing, and positive wealth effects. Within households, ideology does not combine linearly: mixed-ideology couples transact less than politically homogeneous ones, and their choices align more with the man’s ideology.
papers.summary: Research in psychology suggests that conservatives should focus more on the investment value of durables, whereas liberals on consumption value. We test this hypothesis by examining the differential housing transaction motives of conservative and liberal households. Similar to other durable goods, housing assets embody both consumption and investment values and represent the largest assets of U.S. households.

papers.title: Do Equity Markets Spur Corporate Detox?
papers.abstract: This paper provides archival and experimental evidence that equity market feedback influences firms' environmental behavior. Following the publication of U.S. Reports on Carcinogens, firms using newly identified carcinogens that experience particularly negative stock-price reactions reduce toxic waste more, especially when their worker exposure is high. Cross-sectional tests show stronger effects where market signals are likely to be more informative, and peer-firm evidence suggests that firms also learn from affected firms' stock-price reactions. We complement the archival evidence with an information provision experiment using participants with managerial experience in TRI-reporting industries. Participants assigned randomly to a negative stock-market signal are more likely to state that they would undertake costly toxic-release reductions and abatement. Overall, while existing research emphasizes divestment and engagement, this paper highlights an additional mechanism through which financial markets shape corporate responsibility: prices convey information that managers use to adjust environmental practices.
papers.keywords: ESG; Feedback effect; Learning; Institutional investors; Peer effects; Social capital; Toxic waste releases; Experiments; JEL: G12; G20; J01; R10

papers.title: The Foreign Currency Risk of International Remittances
papers.abstract: We study the role of foreign currency risk in remittance markets, and its consequences for fees and market structure. Because operators quote fees before settling transfers, exchange rate risk that is costly to hedge in thin currency markets enters their marginal cost, keeping fees high even in competitive corridors. We test this using 34,680 cash-to-cash products across 339 corridors between 2011 and 2024. We find that fees rise with currency risk, both in conditional variation across corridors and after a volatility shock originating outside the corridor, exploiting the Swiss National Bank's 2015 abandonment of the franc's euro floor and subsequent carry trade reversal. Operators respond by adjusting the variable fee rather than the fixed one, especially in thin hedging markets and for operators geographically concentrated. Currency risk also lowers operator profits and induces corridor exit. A structural model attributes 16 percent of remittance fees to currency risk, comparable to the contribution of market power.
papers.summary: We study the role of foreign currency risk in remittance markets, and its consequences for fees and market structure. Because operators quote fees before settling transfers, exchange rate risk that is costly to hedge in thin currency markets enters their marginal cost, keeping fees high even in competitive corridors. We test this using 34,680 cash-to-cash products across 339 corridors between 2011 and 2024.

papers.title: When Cash Flows Turn Negative: Liquidity-Driven Selling by Pension Funds
papers.abstract: Pension funds are long-horizon investors with predictable liability structures. As such, they are often perceived as investors who can provide liquidity and stabilize markets. However, pension funds increasingly face negative operating cash flows as benefit payments exceed contributions. Using aggregate data on U.S. public pension funds combined with granular holdings obtained through public records requests, we document three findings that challenge the conventional view of pension funds as stabilizing investors. First, pension funds with more negative cash flows do not adjust their target asset allocations and maintain low allocations to safe and liquid assets. Second, because of these limited safe asset buffers, pension funds meet cash flow shocks primarily by selling equities, absorbing $0.67 per dollar of shock through equity sales. At the security level, pension funds sell across equities rather than following a safe and liquid-assets-first approach. Third, pension funds sell equities even when equity returns are negative, indicating that these trades reflect liquidity needs rather than portfolio rebalancing. Together, these findings show that pension funds have become regular sellers in equity markets rather than contrarian, stabilizing investors.
papers.keywords: Liquidity; JEL: G11; G23
papers.summary: Pension funds are long-horizon investors with predictable liability structures. As such, they are often perceived as investors who can provide liquidity and stabilize markets. However, pension funds increasingly face negative operating cash flows as benefit payments exceed contributions.

papers.title: The Price of Position: Spatial Equilibrium in the Geostationary Arc
papers.abstract: How costly is uniform congestion pricing when locations differ in value? I study the geostationary orbit, where satellites serve different markets from recorded positions and supported $77 billion in satellite television revenues in 2023. I estimate a spatial model of commercial entry in which efficient charges rise with demand. In the baseline estimates, the optimal uniform charge captures 66 percent of the attainable welfare gain, or 79 percent when income replaces population as the demand measure. It reduces congestion but ends entry at positions accounting for less than a tenth of modeled efficient surplus. Longitude-specific charges recover the rest while preserving entry at marginal positions. Most additional gains arise at positions the uniform charge keeps active. Correcting underpricing at high-demand positions contributes the largest share. Substantial spatial heterogeneity can therefore coexist with large gains from a common price, whose cost depends on the surplus exposed to its pricing errors.
papers.keywords: Spatial equilibrium; JEL: D23; L96; Q20; R12; H23
papers.summary: How costly is uniform congestion pricing when locations differ in value? I study the geostationary orbit, where satellites serve different markets from recorded positions and supported $77 billion in satellite television revenues in 2023. I estimate a spatial model of commercial entry in which efficient charges rise with demand.

papers.title: Who Controls the Defence Industry?
papers.abstract: Defence markets exhibit extreme asset specificity and bilateral monopoly. Transaction-cost economics predicts state ownership or control in such circumstances. This paper examines what governments actually do. Ownership alone does not determine control. A state with zero equity can still have influence through governance provisions and legal tools. Using large language model extraction from annual reports, supplemented by hand-coding, we compile a leximetric dataset on corporate governance and state control for 107 of the world's largest defence companies, drawn from the SIPRI Top 100 for 2022–2024, in 24 countries. We construct a novel State Influence Index (SII) aggregating voting power, voting enhancements, board appointment and veto rights. State ownership is bimodal: full state ownership at one end, no state ownership at the other. Formal control varies independently. China and Russia combine full ownership with full control. The United States has no ownership and little formal control, relying instead on security agreements, revenue dependence and personnel interchange. The rest of the distribution is dispersed. Some countries combine minority equity with legal devices that amplify formal control well beyond ownership stakes. Others rely on regulatory mechanisms with little or no formal governance authority. In several cases, states have delegated control to domestic families operating under implicit state leverage. A complementary State Restraint Index shows that European companies with high state influence tend also to score higher on voluntary self-limitation, consistent with credible commitment to attract private capital. Cross-border cooperation is producing new governance architectures that partition operations across national subsidiaries to reconcile economies of scale with sovereign control. Corporate governance mechanisms matter most when defence entities operate beyond the home state's jurisdiction, where regulatory authority alone does not reach. The patterns are consistent with transaction-cost and property-rights reasoning about asset specificity and bilateral dependence, although the institutional form of state control varies with legal tradition and political economy.

papers.title: Monetary Policy Uncertainty and Bank Credit Allocation
papers.abstract: We analyze how monetary policy uncertainty (MPU) affects bank credit allocation. First, we develop a theoretical model in which MPU consumes banks’ risk-bearing capacity. Higher MPU therefore curbs risky lending, most strongly at less capitalized banks. Second, we test this prediction across U.S. credit markets using FOMC-announcement changes in option implied rate uncertainty, controlling for the monetary policy stance. In syndicated lending, a one standard deviation increase in MPU widens the gap between high- and low-capital banks in lending to riskier relative to safer borrowers by 1.65 percent. Small business and mortgage originations show similar patterns, consistent with this mechanism.

papers.summary: We analyze how monetary policy uncertainty (MPU) affects bank credit allocation. First, we develop a theoretical model in which MPU consumes banks’ risk-bearing capacity. Higher MPU therefore curbs risky lending, most strongly at less capitalized banks.

papers.title: Geopolitics and Rule-Based Trade
papers.abstract: We analyze the stability of rule-based trade when trading partners differ in their geopolitical objectives. We show that asymmetric gains from trade and geopolitical benefits can generate asymmetric equilibria in which one country infringes and the other tolerates the violation even though there is repeated trade. Crucially, cooperation cannot be sustained when retaliation is more costly to the injured country than tolerating the infringement. Rule-based trade, therefore, requires not only sufficiently patient partners but also sufficiently severe losses from infringement relative to the gains from continued trade. The analysis highlights how geopolitics induce fundamental limitations of trade agreements.
papers.keywords: asymmetric equilibrium; rule-based trade; Trade agreements; infringements; Enforcement; JEL: C73; D74; F13; F51
papers.summary: We analyze the stability of rule-based trade when trading partners differ in their geopolitical objectives. We show that asymmetric gains from trade and geopolitical benefits can generate asymmetric equilibria in which one country infringes and the other tolerates the violation even though there is repeated trade.

papers.title: A Network Approach to Geopolitics
papers.abstract: We develop a tractable framework for analyzing geopolitics as a network of coordination and strategic influence. Countries choose geopolitical actions that trade off domestic interests against incentives to align with connected countries. They can exert costly bilateral influence to affect one another's actions. We characterize equilibrium actions and bilateral influence in closed form. Cross-country differences in domestic interests decompose into latent geopolitical cleavages, each of which the network transmits into geopolitical actions independently of the others. The cross-country covariance matrices of domestic interests and of geopolitical actions identify the cleavages and their importance, from which we recover the network. We implement the framework using data on United Nations voting and democratic orientation. The inferred network is well approximated by a few dimensions, aligns with external measures of geopolitical ties, and recovers well-known historical cleavages. We undertake counterfactuals for domestic interests and network connections and quantify three notions of geopolitical power.

papers.title: Understanding Migration Responses to Local Shocks
papers.abstract: A commonly used migration regression relates population changes to local labor demand shocks, often yielding small or statistically insignificant coefficients despite sizable effects on labor market outcomes. We argue that such findings need not imply that mobility is unresponsive to local economic conditions. Rather, conventional migration regressions can be biased, as they do not reflect how workers choose among competing locations. In a parsimonious equilibrium model, local population growth depends on differences between local shocks and those in relevant destinations; when these shocks are correlated, estimated responses are attenuated. Moreover, with industry-level shocks, standard shift-share measures misrepresent locations’ effective exposure, leading to further attenuation. Using simulation experiments based on Brazilian and German administrative data, we show attenuation can exceed 50% and that conventional regression estimates can be highly imprecise. We propose theory-grounded empirical approaches that correct the biases, deliver estimates with a clear structural interpretation, and improve the precision of estimated mobility responses.
papers.keywords: Internal migration; Local labor markets; Local labor demand shocks; Shift-share designs; Spatial spillovers; Sectoral mobility; JEL: R23; J61; C21; F16
papers.summary: A commonly used migration regression relates population changes to local labor demand shocks, often yielding small or statistically insignificant coefficients despite sizable effects on labor market outcomes. papers.title: The Distribution of Automation Rents with Centralized Bargaining
papers.abstract: When technical progress arises from the decreasing cost of machines performing tasks that are highly substitutable with some type of labor, perfect competition may exacerbate wage inequality and concentrate the benefits of economic growth on the workers who are performing less routine tasks. I study how centralized efficient bargaining reallocates automation-generated surplus across technologically heterogeneous worker groups (performing "routine" and "non-routine" tasks) and show that this redistribution can reverse the sign of the relationship between routine workers' productivity and their wage, although this may entail efficiency costs in terms of some unemployment for routine workers and excess investment in automation. I provide conditions for which the efficient bargaining wages are increasing in automation efficiency and show that routine labor employment may increase as automation gets cheaper and the efficiency cost of centralized bargaining gets very small when automation and routine labor are highly substitutable.

papers.title: The Role of Organization in Firm-Sponsored Training
papers.abstract: Some firms are more likely than others to invest in workers’ skills. We document this phenomenon and discuss its implications in light of models of firm-sponsored skills training. The data show that better managed firms, even in the same industries and labor markets, are more likely to train, while training clusters around either managerial or frontline worker development. We argue that organizational differences provide incentives for firms to train beyond traditional explanations that focus on labor market frictions. We illustrate how organizational heterogeneity can generate training investments through a knowledge hierarchy framework where top managers with different skills build bespoke organizations tailored to their unique needs. This in turn makes general skill firm-specific, allowing firms to capture returns on training investment.
papers.keywords: Firm-sponsored training; On-the-job training; Management practices; Knowledge hierarchies; Organizational design; Human capital; JEL: M53; J24; L23; M54
papers.summary: Some firms are more likely than others to invest in workers’ skills. We document this phenomenon and discuss its implications in light of models of firm-sponsored skills training. papers.title: Competitive Centrality: Equilibrium and Comparative Statics in Networks
papers.abstract: We study equilibrium behavior and the propagation of local shocks in networked competition. We introduce competitive centrality, a nonlinear centrality measure that is uniquely determined by network primitives and provides a sufficient statistic for equilibrium behavior. It determines players’ effort allocations and winning probabilities in each bilateral competition. We then use competitive centrality to derive exact expressions for equilibrium responses to local shocks and characterize their signs. Local shocks propagate along network paths according to players’ relative competitive positions. Although these responses can be non-monotone, a simple sign rule determines whether a shock raises or lowers competitive centrality and effort along a propagation path. Together, these results show how network structure and relative competitive positions shape equilibrium responses to local shocks. Interventions that appear to reduce competition—including removing players or links and imposing effort caps—can therefore have unintended consequences elsewhere in the network.

papers.title: Tax Productivity and Economic Development: A Quantitative Macroeconomic Analysis
papers.abstract: This paper examines the role of government capacity to collect taxes in driving economic development. We first draw on a new macro-historical database to document that tax collections relative to tax administration expenditures rise sharply with GDP per capita. We then interpret this finding in a neoclassical growth model with a tax administration sector in which labor inputs are required to raise tax revenues. Countries differ in their levels of tax productivity, capturing how effectively labor is used to raise taxes, as well as their levels of productivity in creating consumption and investment goods. Governments use tax revenues to provide public capital that complements private factors in production and to make transfers. Quantitatively, our model predicts that increases in tax productivity in low-income economies can raise GDP per capita substantially more than suggested by Hulten’s theorem.

papers.title: The Labor Market Effects of GLP-1s: Evidence from Weight Management and Diabetes Cohorts
papers.abstract: Using population-wide administrative microdata from Denmark, we provide the first comprehensive empirical evaluation contrasting the causal labor market effects of GLP-1 receptor agonists across their dual therapeutic tracks: a subsidized diabetic cohort (Ozempic) subject to public reimbursement, and a weight-management cohort (Wegovy) paying entirely out-of-pocket. Exploiting variation in individual prescription timing among eventual users, and validated by a battery of robustness checks leveraging treatment dropouts, alternative insulin baselines, and matched stacked designs, we find robust labor supply expansions that sharply differ by track. For the subsidized diabetes cohort, treatment initiation raises the probability of employment by 4.1 percentage points and quarterly hours worked by 19.5 hours. Conversely, for out-of-pocket weight-management cohorts, employment effects are flat, but the intensive labor supply expands by 29.7 hours per quarter conditional on employment. Wage effects are statistically insignificant across tracks, confirming that labor earnings gains are quantity-driven. Integrating these micro-elasticities into a public finance accounting framework, we show that price regulations shrink the standalone diabetic deficit, while weight-management cohorts generate substantial, pure income tax windfalls that naturally stabilize public health budgets.

papers.title: Non-Academic Criteria for Admission to Israeli Medical Schools: Recommendations for Change
papers.abstract: Three of the top medical schools in Israel (Hebrew University, Tel Aviv University, and the Technion) use the so-called "MOR—MIRKAM" exam as the non-academic criterion in their medical school admissions. Candidates who clear the demanding cognitive thresholds at these three universities are then evaluated at a second stage by one of two assessment centers (MOR or MIRKAM) administered by the National Institute for Testing and Evaluation (NITE). In the final admission score, the Hebrew University places a 60% weight on the MOR—MIRKAM exam and 40% on the cognitive scores, while Tel Aviv University and the Technion weigh the MOR—MIRKAM exam 70% against 30% for the cognitive scores. These are very large weights on an exam without any supporting empirical evidence in Israel that the exam measures clinical skills. The cognitive component includes two measures: (1) the "Bagrut", an exam taken at the end of secondary education in Israel that includes all of the subjects studied in high school and (2) the "Psychometric" Exam, a general scholastic aptitude test with verbal, quantitative, and English sections. The paper first examines the mechanics of the MOR—MIRKAM system. It then discusses the large private industry that charges thousands of dollars to prepare students for the exam. Next the paper explains why the limited empirical work does not test whether the exam measures clinical skills. Finally, the paper recommends changes to how the exam is used to ensure that candidates with the strongest academic records and the greatest research potential are admitted to medical school.
papers.keywords: medical school admissions; multiple mini-interview (MMI); Israel; JEL: I1
papers.summary: Three of the top medical schools in Israel (Hebrew University, Tel Aviv University, and the Technion) use the so-called "MOR—MIRKAM" exam as the non-academic criterion in their medical school admissions.

papers.title: Improved Optimal Investment and Consumption Strategies under Inflation Risk with Stochastic Volatility
papers.abstract: This paper develops and calibrates a financial market model that incorporates stochastic volatility in inflation, interest rate and equity dynamics. Traditional models typically assume constant inflation volatility, which limits investors’ responsiveness to economic shifts as a result of geopolitical tensions and events such as the COVID-19 pandemic. Our multidimensional affine model structure therefore extends the classical Brennan and Xia (2002) framework with a macroeconomic stochastic variance component that allows the model to capture the interdependence of asset price returns and inflation dynamics. Because the premium associated with macroeconomic risks is not directly observable and may vary with the level of uncertainty, we consider multiple model specifications that differ in how bond risk premia depend on this level. We make three contributions. First, we show how to determine optimal consumption and portfolio strategies for finite-horizon investors with constant relative risk aversion risk preferences, by solving the extended version of the Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman equation numerically. Secondly, we demonstrate that taking account of stochastic volatility in these strategies yields substantial welfare gains. A key difference from strategies that do not account for a stochastic variance component is that the sensitivities of the optimal portfolio value to both inflation and equity price shocks decrease with the level of macroeconomic uncertainty. Finally, our sensitivity analyses confirm the robustness of the observed welfare gains for various model specifications and different data periods. Conditioning consumption and investment strategies on the level of macroeconomic uncertainty is welfare enhancing even when the parameters governing its dynamics cannot be perfectly estimated.
papers.keywords: stochastic volatility; JEL: G10; G11; E44
papers.summary: This paper develops and calibrates a financial market model that incorporates stochastic volatility in inflation, interest rate and equity dynamics. Traditional models typically assume constant inflation volatility, which limits investors’ responsiveness to economic shifts as a result of geopolitical tensions and events such as the COVID-19 pandemic.

papers.title: Multimarket Contact and the Southwest Effect: Twenty-Five Years of Evolving Rivalry in the US Airline Industry
papers.abstract: This paper aims to better understand competitive rivalry in the US airline industry over the last 25 years. First, it contributes to a better understanding of the procompetitive "Southwest effect" over the period 2000-2025. We show that this effect can clearly be identified during the first part of our sample period, but disappears circa 2016, when Southwest culminated a process of strategic re-orientation and appears to have started behaving like legacy carriers. Second, we find that Southwest presence on a route flattened the relationship between air fares and Multimarket Contact (MMC) until the mid-2010s; since then, the two groups of routes have converged. Third, we document that the effect of MMC on fares has diminished over time. We conjecture that this may be due to increased concentration and symmetry among major players. Fourth, our results indicate that a linear specification to identify the relationship between MMC and fares may be adequate until 2007. This is no longer the case afterwards: the data point to a non-monotonic U/V-like shape, first on routes with Southwest and, from 2016, on all routes. Fifth, the pandemic seems to have led to a temporary breakdown in tacit collusion, but only on routes where Southwest was not present; once the COVID-19 crisis ended, the long-run evolution of the MMC–fare relationship resumed.

papers.summary: This paper aims to better understand competitive rivalry in the US airline industry over the last 25 years. First, it contributes to a better understanding of the procompetitive "Southwest effect" over the period 2000-2025.

papers.title: Personalized Pricing and the Value of Past Purchase Histories: An Empirical Perspective
papers.abstract: Grocery loyalty programs record purchase histories that retailers do not use to personalize prices. We measure how much they forgo with a structural model of demand and pricing in which a Bayesian seller learns preferences from past purchases and personalizes prices. Profits rise by 7.1\% with one-year histories, capturing two thirds of the gains under perfect knowledge of preferences. Most consumers (84.1\%) gain, but the losses of the minority outweigh these gains, and aggregate consumer surplus falls. An optimal loyalty program charges a membership fee, yet most consumers enroll, because opting out signals price insensitivity.

papers.title: Dynamic Factor Models and Cointegration
papers.abstract: The factors of a stationary Dynamic Factor Model (DFM) are the first differences of singular I(1) processes. Being singular, such processes are always cointegrated. This however does not prevent the existence of a VAR for their first differences, so that the standard estimation procedure of the stationary DFM remains valid. Problems arise only when there is a linear combination of the shocks that has transitory effects on all the variables of the panel. We argue that this case is implausible for macroeconomic data and show that in fact it does not occur for two widely used US data sets — the FRED-QD and the FRED-MD. A Monte Carlo exercise shows that the standard procedure outperforms alternative methods based on the factors in levels, especially at long horizons.

papers.title: Beyond Digital Rights: An Institutional Architecture for Consumer Empowerment
papers.abstract: Digital governance has substantially expanded consumers' formal rights over personal data, yet these rights often fail to translate into effective agency in digital markets. We identify this as an institutional capability gap: individual consumers lack the information, expertise, accountability mechanisms, and bargaining capacity required to exercise legal rights continuously and economically effectively. We develop the Innovation in the Digital Economy Architecture (IDEA) as an institutional response. Rather than proposing additional substantive rights, IDEA integrates four mutually reinforcing mechanisms: consumer control over personal data anchored by verified Key Personal Data; accredited expert representation; fiduciary governance of delegated authority; and collective negotiation over data-processing arrangements. The novelty lies not primarily in these mechanisms individually, each of which has institutional precedents, but in their complementarity within a single governance architecture: control enables authorisation, representation supplies expertise, fiduciary duties discipline delegation, and collective negotiation converts dispersed rights into organised market agency. IDEA thereby shifts digital governance from reliance predominantly on individual consent and ex-post regulatory enforcement toward continuing institutionalised consumer participation. By embedding consumer agency within market processes, the framework seeks to make trustworthy data governance a dimension of competition and innovation. The paper contributes an institutional theory of digital consumer empowerment linking information systems, digital governance, institutional economics, and market design.
papers.keywords: Consumer empowerment; Digital governance; Institutional architecture; Personal data governance; Key Personal Data; Fiduciary duties; JEL: D23; D82; L14; L86; O33; O38; P48; K24

papers.title: Divisive by Design: Shaping Values in Optimal Mechanisms
papers.abstract: We study a principal who allocates a good to agents with private, independently distributed values through an optimal mechanism. The principal can strategically shape these value distributions by modifying the good’s features, which affect agents’ valuations. Our analysis reveals that optimal designs are frequently divisive – creating goods that appeal strongly to specific agents or agent types while being less valued by others. These divisive designs reduce information rents and increase total surplus, even though they reduce competition. Even when total surplus is constrained, some divisiveness in designs remains optimal.
papers.keywords: Differentiation; JEL: D82; D46; L15
papers.summary: We study a principal who allocates a good to agents with private, independently distributed values through an optimal mechanism. The principal can strategically shape these value distributions by modifying the good’s features, which affect agents’ valuations.

papers.title: Foreign Giants' Broad Shoulders: The Causal Effect of Foreign Ideas on U.S. Innovation
papers.abstract: We study the role of foreign ideas in U.S. innovation by constructing a directed “genealogy” of technologies from the full text of 13 million patents filed between 1894 and 2024. By tracing which earlier technologies appear in the founding patents of new ones, we recover a large-scale input–output network of technological recombination that identifies the foreign technologies that serve as inputs into innovation in the United States. We report four main findings. First, foreign ideas are pervasive: 56% ofU.S.technologies build on at least one foreign input, and the most fertile U.S. technologies rely on foreign inputs most heavily. Second, foreign ideas have large causal effects on U.S. innovation. Using the historical settlement of migrants as a source of exogenous variation in local ancestry, we show that U.S. counties more exposed to knowledge from a given foreign country absorb substantially more technologies from that country and, in turn, invent significantly more U.S. technologies building on them. Third, foreign ideas shape not only the level but also the direction of technical change: U.S. counties are far more likely to pioneer the specific technologies whose foreign inputs are already in their local idea stock, and the changing origins of foreign ideas accompany the shift of American innovation from its historical heartland toward the coasts. Fourth, these effects leave a lasting imprint on local labor markets: decades later, counties that absorbed more of an origin’s ideas host more jobs working with those ideas, and even more work with the U.S. technologies descended from them.
papers.keywords: Technology diffusion; Innovation; Knowledge spillover; Migration; Ancestry; JEL: O33; O31; F22; J15; R12; O34
papers.summary: We study the role of foreign ideas in U.S. innovation by constructing a directed “genealogy” of technologies from the full text of 13 million patents filed between 1894 and 2024.

papers.title: This Time It's Different: The Role of Women's Employment in Recessions
papers.abstract: We study the transmission of macroeconomic shocks in a model of the household sector featuring single and married households, joint labor-supply decisions of women and men, and childcare needs that interact with the availability of remote work. Recessions concentrated among women are deeper and more persistent than those concentrated among men, reflecting weaker within-family insurance and a new empirical finding that women re-enter employment more slowly after job loss. Yet recovery from the pandemic recession, which had a disproportionate impact on working women due to school closures and the sectoral distribution of job losses, was surprisingly rapid. We show that in our model, the expansion of remote work and shifting caregiving norms after the pandemic raise female labor supply and men's share of childcare, thereby accounting for the observed recovery. These changes permanently increase female participation and narrow the gender earnings gap, but their effect on future recessions is limited: greater labor force attachment among women weakens the added-worker effect but also accelerates labor market re-entry, leading to offsetting effects on aggregate recession dynamics.
papers.keywords: Added worker effect; Recessions
papers.summary: We study the transmission of macroeconomic shocks in a model of the household sector featuring single and married households, joint labor-supply decisions of women and men, and childcare needs that interact with the availability of remote work.

papers.title: Risk Management in Monetary Policy: A Review with Asset Pricing Implications
papers.abstract: We review recent research on how the Fed's risk-management approach shapes the overall policy stance and how it affects financial market conditions. The evidence shows that the policy stance contains a forward-looking, conditional component that has long been an integral part of the Fed's policymaking toolkit. Asymmetric forward-looking policy tilts — motivated by risk-management considerations and revealed via the Fed's communication — complement and extend beyond the effects of direct policy actions. Drawing on the transcripts of FOMC meetings between 1976 and 2019, we provide an institutional history of the tilt and its connection to how the Committee's thinking about risk evolved over decades. Going back at least to the early 1990s, the Fed has relied on tilts not only to steer market expectations but, equally importantly, to stabilize risk premia and maintain easy financial conditions. We discuss successes and challenges associated with communication via tilts and draw lessons for the renewed debate over the form and extent of central bank forward-looking guidance.
papers.keywords: Monetary policy; Federal Reserve; Risk management; Term premia; Central bank communication; JEL: E52; E58; G12; E43; N12
papers.summary: We review recent research on how the Fed's risk-management approach shapes the overall policy stance and how it affects financial market conditions. The evidence shows that the policy stance contains a forward-looking, conditional component that has long been an integral part of the Fed's policymaking toolkit.

papers.title: Infinite Factor Structure in Conditional Asset Pricing
papers.abstract: The return covariance matrix is widely assumed to have an eigenvalue cliff: a few large eigenvalues, then a bounded bulk, as in the approximate factor structure of Chamberlain and Rothschild (1983). This premise underlies factor tests, principal-component methods, and large-covariance estimation. These methods estimate moments from returns pooled across states, so they necessarily view a conditional world unconditionally. We show that, generically, this view removes the cliff: a conditional model with a few factors is, unconditionally, an infinite-factor model in which infinitely many eigenvalues diverge. This holds for the characteristic-managed portfolios that machine-learning methods trade, and for individual stocks whose loadings differ persistently across firms. Yet as long as conditional expected returns admit no asymptotic arbitrage, the maximal Sharpe ratio stays finite. For generic expected returns, infinitely many components are priced, so no finite set of principal components spans expected returns. Reducing returns to a few principal components therefore discards priced risk.
papers.keywords: JEL: G12; C38; C58

papers.title: Female Jobs and Fertility: Long-term Experimental Evidence from Ethiopian Factories
papers.abstract: We conducted an experiment with multiple factories in Ethiopia to test the widespread hypothesis that formal employment among women reduces fertility. Tracking respondents over eight years, we find that women who were randomly offered a job had more children than the control group. The effect on fertility emerged once the effect on wage employment faded away, around three years after baseline. There are clear effects on household income and savings, but not on bargaining power or marriage. These patterns are consistent with a Beckerian model in which the income effect dominates the substitution effect and households are credit constrained.
papers.keywords: Female employment; Fertility; Industrialization; Sub-saharan africa; JEL: J13; J16; J22; O15; O55

papers.title: Central Bank Losses and Inflation: 350 Years of Evidence
papers.abstract: Are central bank losses inflationary? We show in a simple model that, absent fiscal support, large losses can create a trade-off between stabilizing inflation and stabilizing central bank net worth. We then provide evidence that central bank net worth matters for monetary policy in practice, drawing on a new historical data set with more than 350 years of annual data for Sweden and its central bank, the Riksbank. Using a narrative approach, we identify large adverse shocks to the Riksbank's profitability and trace their dynamic effects. They raise inflation persistently under fiat but not under metallic standards. Moreover, adverse import-price shocks generate more inflation and a more accommodative monetary response when central bank net worth is low. This historical evidence therefore bears directly on current debates over the monetary-policy consequences of large and risky central-bank balance sheets.
papers.keywords: Inflation; JEL: E52; E58; N13; N14
papers.summary: Are central bank losses inflationary? papers.title: At-Risk or Responsive? Targeting in Unemployment Policy
papers.abstract: This paper evaluates the use of algorithmic risk profiling to direct job search support toward individuals most at risk of long-term unemployment. Using three regression discontinuity designs and rich administrative data from the Flemish Public Employment Service (VDAB) in Belgium, we address two key dimensions: whom and when to target. First, job search counseling raises employment on average, but treatment effects decline sharply with predicted risk. This reveals a fundamental trade-off between targeting those most at risk and those most responsive to intervention. Second, we find no evidence that treatment effects depreciate at the individual level, but strong dynamic selection: as spells lengthen, surviving job seekers have both higher baseline risk and lower treatment responsiveness, with opposing implications for the returns to treatment. We develop and calibrate a conceptual framework for optimal targeting that highlights the key role of the ratio of predicted treatment effects to predicted job-finding probabilities. Targeting rules combining both objects substantially outperform the status quo, yielding welfare gains nearly three times as large as those from random assignment, while targeting on risk scores alone performs worse than random assignment.
papers.keywords: Unemployment; Targeting; Treatment Effect Heterogeneity; Regression discontinuity; Public employment services; Machine learning; JEL: J64; J65; H43; C21
papers.summary: This paper evaluates the use of algorithmic risk profiling to direct job search support toward individuals most at risk of long-term unemployment. Using three regression discontinuity designs and rich administrative data from the Flemish Public Employment Service (VDAB) in Belgium, we address two key dimensions: whom and when to target.

papers.title: Intra-Household Insurance and the Intergenerational Transmission of Income Risk
papers.abstract: This paper studies the mechanisms and the extent to which parental wage risk passes through to children’s skill development. Through a quantitative dynamic labor supply model in which two parents choose whether to work short or long hours or not work at all, time spent with children, and child-related expenditures, we find that increased wage risk reduces children’s skill levels at the end of childhood. To the extent that making up for cognitive skill losses during childhood is hard—as available evidence suggests—uninsurable income risk can negatively impact the labor market prospects of future generations.
papers.summary: This paper studies the mechanisms and the extent to which parental wage risk passes through to children’s skill development. Through a quantitative dynamic labor supply model in which two parents choose whether to work short or long hours or not work at all, time spent with children, and child-related expenditures, we find that increased wage risk reduces children’s skill levels at the end of childhood.

papers.title: Who Can Produce What? Firm Capabilities and Product Entry
papers.abstract: Which firms supply which products? Modeling multi-product firms under heterogeneous markups, we recover firms’ costs for produced products and develop an algorithm inspired by recommender systems to predict costs for unproduced products. Lower predicted costs imply increased product adoption and identify which firms enter when export demand rises, including firms crossing broad product classifications. We use these counterfactual costs to quantify how reductions in fixed and marginal costs induce product entry and lower price indices. In a price-stabilization exercise following a cost shock, entry subsidies can cost less than subsidies to incumbents, particularly for smaller shocks when capable potential entrants remain available.
papers.keywords: Multi-product firms; JEL: F1; F6; D2; L1
papers.summary: Which firms supply which products? Modeling multi-product firms under heterogeneous markups, we recover firms’ costs for produced products and develop an algorithm inspired by recommender systems to predict costs for unproduced products. papers.title: Who Benefits from Market Concentration? The Effects of Hospital Mergers on Physician Income
papers.abstract: We examine the effect of hospital mergers on the income of medical specialists, with a specific focus on how this effect varies across different contractual arrangements between hospitals and medical specialists. We analyze the effects of 17 mergers that occurred in the Netherlands between 2011 and 2018. Using administrative data and employing a difference-in-differences empirical approach, we find that hospital mergers increase the income of self-employed medical specialists by 3.86\% and do not affect the income of salaried medical specialists. Among the self-employed, mergers lead to significant income increases for men, more senior physicians, and those with the highest incomes prior to the merger. These results are in line with our theoretical model. Furthermore, we do not find significant effects on hospital expenditures and 30-day mortality, but a reduction in hospital admissions and the number of physicians.
papers.keywords: physician income; Bargaining power; Hospital mergers; medical specialists; JEL: I11; L44; J31
papers.summary: We examine the effect of hospital mergers on the income of medical specialists, with a specific focus on how this effect varies across different contractual arrangements between hospitals and medical specialists. We analyze the effects of 17 mergers that occurred in the Netherlands between 2011 and 2018.

papers.title: Do Judges Move Markets? Ideological Shifts in the Supreme Court and Macroeconomic Expectations
papers.abstract: This paper studies how judicial ideology shapes financial markets' expectations about the macroeconomy. We use unexpected deaths of U.S. Supreme Court Justices as quasi-experimental shifts in the Court's ideological balance. High-frequency asset price responses reveal how markets perceive the macroeconomic consequences of these ideological shifts. We find that a more conservative Court is associated with lower inflation expectations, lower real activity expectations, and lower bond yields. A shift towards a more liberal Court induces the opposite responses. The finding that inflation and activity expectations respond with the same sign suggests that markets revise their expectations about aggregate demand, rather than aggregate supply. Moreover, contrasting the yield responses with estimates from studies of fiscal policy news indicates that a more conservative (liberal) Court leads markets to expect tighter (looser) future fiscal policy. We validate our quasi-experimental setup with sectoral asset price dynamics, such as high-frequency responses of clean energy and health care stocks. Taken together, our findings are consistent with markets interpreting changes in the Supreme Court's ideological composition as news about future fiscal expansions or contractions.
papers.keywords: Supreme Court; High-frequency identification; Expectations; News shocks; Fiscal policy; JEL: E31; E32; D72; K40
papers.summary: This paper studies how judicial ideology shapes financial markets' expectations about the macroeconomy. We use unexpected deaths of U.S. Supreme Court Justices as quasi-experimental shifts in the Court's ideological balance. papers.title: Optimal Unconventional Policy in a New Keynesian Preferred Habitat Model
papers.abstract: We study conventional and balance sheet policy in a general equilibrium model with heterogeneous households, nominal rigidities, and limits to arbitrage. Both instruments move risk prices through portfolio rebalancing; because household portfolios differ in duration, the induced term premium fluctuations lower welfare through imperfect risk-sharing. Conservative calibrations imply these welfare costs are comparable to or larger than those of traditional stabilization motives. When divine coincidence holds and both instruments are unconstrained, optimal policy satisfies a separation principle: conventional policy stabilizes output and inflation, while balance sheet policy stabilizes term premia. If the short rate is constrained, balance sheet policy is a necessary but imperfect tool for macroeconomic stabilization; with costly balance sheet tools, a less reactive short rate improves welfare at the cost of greater macroeconomic volatility. Under commitment, the path of the short rate can mitigate households' exposure to aggregate risk. Our results justify a central bank "triple mandate" that includes term premia alongside output and inflation, and challenge the view that balance sheet policy is a close substitute for the short rate.
papers.summary: We study conventional and balance sheet policy in a general equilibrium model with heterogeneous households, nominal rigidities, and limits to arbitrage. Both instruments move risk prices through portfolio rebalancing; because household portfolios differ in duration, the induced term premium fluctuations lower welfare through imperfect risk-sharing.

papers.title: Bayesian Inference for Heteroskedastic Proxy-SVARs
papers.abstract: We develop a Bayesian posterior simulation method for SVAR models characterized by conditionally heteroskedastic shocks and nontriangular zero restrictions, a class that includes Proxy-SVARs as a special case. The method embeds a conditional Sequential Monte Carlo (SMC) step within a Gibbs sampler. The SMC step exploits an auxiliary homoskedastic model to construct a proposal density and progressively adapts the corresponding particle distribution to incorporate heteroskedasticity, moving through a sequence of intermediate densities. In Monte Carlo experiments, the sampler recovers the structural parameters and impulse responses and produces narrower intervals than the homoskedastic model. Applications to technology and personal income tax shocks show that allowing for stochastic volatility can reduce posterior uncertainty and alter estimated responses.

papers.title: Valuing Cryptocurrencies: Three Easy Pieces
papers.abstract: Can simple, off-the-shelf models explain positive, persistent, and volatile market valuations of privately issued digital assets? I review ” three easy pieces” - models in which cryptocurrencies can serve as a medium of exchange, a vehicle for saving, and a means of overcoming search and matching frictions in conditional payments. Each functionality imparts positive value, yet interferes with the others. Until these features can be separated, their mutual interference seems likely to inhibit widespread adoption of cryptocurrencies as money.
papers.keywords: Cryptocurrencies; digital assets; Search and matching; Asset pricing; Private money
papers.summary: Can simple, off-the-shelf models explain positive, persistent, and volatile market valuations of privately issued digital assets? I review ” three easy pieces” - models in which cryptocurrencies can serve as a medium of exchange, a vehicle for saving, and a means of overcoming search and matching frictions in conditional payments. Each functionality imparts positive value, yet interferes with the others.

papers.title: From Reagan to Trump: Regional Development Traps and the Remaking of American Electoral Politics
papers.abstract: This paper examines the territorial reconfiguration of American electoral politics since the 1980s, tracing the remaking of Republican support from Reagan’s 1984 landslide to Trump’s three presidential campaigns (2016, 2020, 2024). Drawing on panel data for every presidential election from 1984 to 2024 across 722 commuting zones, we test whether regional development traps, defined as enduring economic underperformance, explain both the shift from Democrats to Republicans and the Republicans’ internal realignment. Mundlak/Correlated Random Effects estimates show backlash is overwhelmingly driven by structural, not cyclical, decline. Short-term economic fluctuations do not predict Republican swing, while long-run territorial position does so decisively. Voters are not responding to recessions. They are registering alienation from an economic order that has failed their communities for a generation. Trump’s gains concentrated in places persistently left behind, whose peripheral position has become entrenched.
papers.summary: This paper examines the territorial reconfiguration of American electoral politics since the 1980s, tracing the remaking of Republican support from Reagan’s 1984 landslide to Trump’s three presidential campaigns (2016, 2020, 2024).

papers.title: Occupational Licensing Without Learning
papers.abstract: Whether earnings premia in licensed occupations reflect human capital or scarcity rents is hard to identify, because training and licensing are bundled. We exploit a reform at Uruguay's main university that shortened the accounting degree and granted a license, without additional learning requirements, to students already working alongside incumbent accountants. Competition from these new licensees identifies changes in licensing rents, separate from returns to training. Incumbent accountants' earnings fell by about 9 percent relative to comparable professionals, with no change in employment, consistent with licensing rents.
papers.keywords: Occupational licensing; JEL: J44; J31; K31; I23; L51

papers.title: Double Selection in Causal Inference
papers.abstract: We introduce a unified double selection framework accommodating group-specific additive and multiplicative shifters of an unobserved common time trend (CTT). Under double selection, the CTT does not manifest as a parallel trend; the resulting non-constant selection bias is a linear combination nesting standard difference-in-differences (DiD) in levels and logs. Opposing shifters can yield patterns structurally impossible under standard DiDs, such as a ranking reversal of the groups over time. We establish that in the presence of double selection bias treatment effects are non-parametrically identified by the change of the ratio of within-group outcome changes over time. The double selection structure induces a stable linear relationship in the outcome-on-outcome space, grounding a simple two-step estimator operating in levels. Revisiting Card (1992), double selection uncovers valid counterfactuals where standard DiD fails.
papers.keywords: Double Selection; Difference-in-differences; Causal inference; Nonparametric identification; JEL: C14; C21; J38
papers.summary: We introduce a unified double selection framework accommodating group-specific additive and multiplicative shifters of an unobserved common time trend (CTT). Under double selection, the CTT does not manifest as a parallel trend; the resulting non-constant selection bias is a linear combination nesting standard difference-in-differences (DiD) in levels and logs.

papers.title: The Economics of Free Bets
papers.abstract: Sportsbooks offer promotional ``free bets'' that return profits if the bets win, but not the stake provided. These bets can be hedged to produce guaranteed profits. This paper shows how to value the guaranteed profit from these stake-not-returned free bets under a simple constant-margin pricing rule in which sportsbooks, on average, keep a fraction m of the money staked. The guaranteed hedged value is a nonlinear function of the free bet's probability of winning, reaching a maximum when this probability is the square root of m time 1-m. Empirical evidence from odds on tennis bets confirms this prediction.

papers.title: Shifting Grounds: Social Norms and the Intergenerational Transmission of Wealth
papers.abstract: How do social norms shape the intergenerational allocation of land, particularly regarding gender equity? We combine experimental and administrative data from Senegal with a model of social interactions to study how parental preferences and community norms influence land allocation to sons and daughters. A choice experiment that randomizes land allocations and normative cues reveals that parents are more responsive to community norms when allocating land to daughters—a pattern subsequently borne out in administrative records. Simulations show that this asymmetry generates multiple equilibria in land allocation to daughters but not sons, so even modest shifts in perceived norms can meaningfully reduce gender gaps.
papers.keywords: JEL: O12; Q15; J16
papers.summary: How do social norms shape the intergenerational allocation of land, particularly regarding gender equity? We combine experimental and administrative data from Senegal with a model of social interactions to study how parental preferences and community norms influence land allocation to sons and daughters.

papers.title: Job Seekers’ Beliefs and Preferences over Wages and Benefits: Experimental Evidence from Online Job Boards
papers.abstract: We estimate how strongly job seekers value wages and job benefits, how well informed they are about compensation differences across employers, and how much they update their beliefs when shown such information. In a field experiment, we randomly embed wage and benefit information from an employer-review platform on job ads for 265,000 users of a Swiss job-board network. The revealed-preference estimates suggest that a 1% higher posted wage increases clicks to view and engage with the ad by 0.4%. A conceptual framework decomposes this elasticity into preferences, prior knowledge, and belief updating, which we identify through a belief-elicitation experiment with users from the same job boards. We find that job seekers underestimate wage differences across jobs by half, know little about benefit differences, and update beliefs only partially. Accounting for these information frictions, the implied own-wage elasticity of applications is 2.5–2.9. Among the twelve benefits shown across the experiment, job seekers value four significantly: a company car (10% of wages), work from home (8%), firm-sponsored childcare (6%), and a parking spot (4%). The average position offers benefits worth 11% of wages. Because higher-paying jobs offer more benefits, inequality in total compensation exceeds wage inequality.
papers.keywords: Amenities; Job Benefits; Job search; Wage Elasticity of Applications; Wage Transparency; Willingness to pay; JEL: J32; J33; J64
papers.summary: We estimate how strongly job seekers value wages and job benefits, how well informed they are about compensation differences across employers, and how much they update their beliefs when shown such information. In a field experiment, we randomly embed wage and benefit information from an employer-review platform on job ads for 265,000 users of a Swiss job-board network.

papers.title: The Hold-Up Problem and Communication: Experimental Evidence
papers.abstract: The hold-up problem plays a central role in organizational and institutional economics. According to standard theory, an investor may have insufficient incentives to invest in a relationship with a trading partner when the investor anticipates that in future negotiations the trading partner might behave opportunistically, so the investor's costs might not be recouped. In a prominent paper-and-pencil experiment, Ellingsen and Johannesson (2004a) have shown that communication can mitigate the hold-up problem. They allow either the investor or the trading partner to send a single text message to the other player. In order to study the robustness of their findings, we replicate their setup in an online experiment, allowing for a larger number of observations and a different subject pool.
